newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Glitches, muddle delay start of Nicaraguan vote.
newsitem.headline: Glitches, muddle delay start of Nicaraguan vote.

text.p: Nicaragua's tense presidential elections began in chaos on Sunday, as technical problems and confusion prevented booths opening on time, keeping angry voters waiting in line for hours.

"I've got no idea of what I should be doing," Pedro Cepeda, an election official, told Reuters as he waited at a booth, one of many that had failed to open an hour after voting was due to have started at 7 a.m. (1300 GMT).

In a staggeringly complex election, 32,000 candidates are on the ballot nationwide, including 23 just for president. Each voter has to tick off a choice on six separate ballots, each running to three feet (one meter) in length.

The two front-runners, right-wing populist Arnoldo Aleman of the Liberal Alliance, and his arch-foe, Sandinista former ruler Daniel Ortega, were expected to finish almost neck and neck, according to opinion polls last week.
The tight race has helped foster a fever to vote in a country whose history was a long saga of dictatorship and war until it embraced peaceful democracy in 1990.

Seeking to placate the population, on Saturday election authorities extended the midday deadline for issuing credentials until late into the night. But election officals said there were still 100,000 eligible voters unregistered.
"We're seeing how complicated the voting procedure is. There are six elections going on simultaneously," said former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, monitoring the vote.
The voting booth where President Violeta Chamorro was due to make her choice for a successor opened two hours late.

A European Union observer mission touring Managua found the first 13 booths it visited had failed to open in the first hour. Frustrated voters waited in long lines outside, many of them there since 4 a.m. They grumbled over the delay but officials said there was nothing they could do about it.
Either materials had not arrived, or election officials failed to turn up, they said.

The delay threatened to put back the first results of the election, which were not expected until early on Monday. Also, the complexity of choosing from such a jumble of candidates in a country where many people are illiterate meant voting proceeded at a snail's pace.
It was expected to be worse in conflictive rural regions.
"Little by little, the elections are getting going. One thing I'm sure about is that they are not going to end (on time) at 6 p.m.," said Dutchman Frans Van Haren, head of the European Union mission.
Election officials said they would extend the deadline until the last person in line had voted.
